detail.scope: Commercial-sector electricity sales and average price by state, as reported to EIA. Data centers are billed mostly in the commercial class, so this is a proxy for their load, not a measurement of it.

analysis.body:
The five grid operators represented here — ERCOT, NYISO, MISO, SPP, and CAISO — collectively show more than 1.3 million megawatts of generation and storage capacity sitting in interconnection queues as of August 31, 2026, spread across 8,378 individual requests. These are proposed projects that have asked to connect to the grid and are working through studies and approvals; they are not data center demand figures, and because each operator defines its queue differently, the totals cannot simply be added together as a single national number. What the queues do reveal is the composition of planned supply that would eventually serve all grid customers, including the data centers concentrated in states like Texas and Virginia that appear among the highest commercial electricity sales in the EIA snapshot.

Battery storage and natural gas are the fuel types most closely watched as signals of data-center-driven load growth, because storage smooths intermittent renewable output and gas provides the firm, dispatchable capacity that large computing loads require around the clock. ERCOT's Texas queue alone shows 160,906 megawatts of storage and 76,751 megawatts of gas among its 440,018 total megawatts, by far the largest gas and storage figures of any operator in this dataset. SPP carries 52,913 megawatts of storage and 47,392 megawatts of gas across 198,716 total megawatts, while MISO shows 68,429 megawatts of storage and 30,236 megawatts of gas across 299,721 megawatts; CAISO's active queue, which excludes completed and withdrawn projects per its scope, holds 46,944 megawatts of storage and only 916 megawatts of gas across 71,682 megawatts. NYISO's fuel breakdown places the vast majority of its 319,095 megawatts in an "other" category, limiting direct comparison on storage and gas.

The EIA commercial electricity sales data for June 2026 offers a partial view of where large power consumers are currently active: Texas leads the eight states reported at 15,754 gigawatt-hours of commercial sales that month, followed by California at 10,025 and Virginia at 7,771, with prices ranging from 8.66 cents per kilowatt-hour in Texas to 27.33 cents in California — a spread that shapes where data center operators choose to locate new capacity. These sales figures are a proxy for, not a measurement of, data center load, since commercial billing covers many customer types. The figure to watch in coming months is whether gas interconnection requests in ERCOT and SPP continue growing faster than solar, which would suggest that firm-capacity needs tied to always-on loads are outpacing the renewable buildout that had dominated queue volumes through most of the early 2020s.
